# Irrational rotation

*Image: Sturmian-sequence-from-irrational-rotation.gif.* Sturmian sequence generated by irrational rotation with theta=0.2882748715208621 and x=0.078943143

::: {#o1 .subject cue=lead name="Irrational rotation"}

An **irrational rotation** in the mathematical theory of [dynamical systems](wikipedia://en/9087), is defined as a [map](wikipedia://en/516931) $f$, as follows:

:::

Let $x\in [0, 1)$ be arbitrary, and let $\theta$ be any irrational number. For $i\in$ $\{0, 1, 2 ...\}$ define[^o2] $f^i_\theta : [0,1) \rightarrow [0,1)$ by

$f^i_\theta(x) = x + i\cdot\theta$ (mod 1)

Under the identification of a [circle](wikipedia://en/6220) with $\mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Z}$, or with the interval $[0, 1)$ with the boundary points glued together, this map becomes a [rotation](wikipedia://en/39789) of a [circle](wikipedia://en/6220) by a proportion $\theta$ of a full revolution (i.e., an angle of $2\pi\theta$ radians). Since $\theta$ is irrational, the rotation has infinite [order](wikipedia://en/493527) in the [circle group](wikipedia://en/508177), and the map $f_{\theta}$ has no [periodic orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_orbit).

Alternatively, we can use multiplicative notation for an irrational rotation by introducing the map

$$f_\theta :S^1 \to S^1, \quad \quad \quad f_\theta(x)=xe^{2\pi i\theta}$$

The relationship between the additive and multiplicative notations is the group isomorphism

$$\varphi:([0,1),+) \to (S^1, \cdot) \quad \varphi(x)=xe^{2\pi i\theta}.$$

It can be shown that $\varphi$ is an [isometry](wikipedia://en/254777).

There is a strong distinction in circle rotations that depends on whether $\theta$ is rational or irrational. Rational rotations are less interesting examples of dynamical systems because if $\theta = \frac{a}{b}$ and $\gcd(a,b) = 1$, then $f_\theta^b(x) = x$ when $x \in [0,1)$. It can also be shown that $f_\theta^i(x) \ne x$ when $1 \le i < b$.

## Significance {#Significance}

Irrational rotations form a fundamental example in the theory of [dynamical systems](wikipedia://en/9087). According to the [Denjoy theorem](wikipedia://en/4257408), every orientation-preserving $C^{2}$-diffeomorphism of the circle with an irrational [rotation number](wikipedia://en/3928569) $\theta$ is [topologically conjugate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topologically_conjugate) to $f_{\theta}$. An irrational rotation is a [measure-preserving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure-preserving_transformation) [ergodic transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_transformation), but it is not [mixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_%28physics%29). The [Poincaré map](wikipedia://en/876732) for the dynamical system associated with the [Kronecker foliation](wikipedia://en/371227#Linear_and_Kronecker_foliations) on a [torus](wikipedia://en/74800) with angle $\theta>$ is the irrational rotation by $\theta$. [C\*-algebras](wikipedia://en/7184) associated with irrational rotations, known as [irrational rotation algebras](wikipedia://en/37990843), have been extensively studied.

::: {#o5 .statement kind=statement/fact cue=heading name="Properties"}

## Properties {#Properties}

- If $\theta$ is irrational, then the orbit of any element of $[0, 1]$ under the rotation $f_{\theta}$ is [dense](wikipedia://en/23523594) in $[0, 1)$. Therefore, irrational rotations are [topologically transitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topologically_transitive).
- Irrational (and rational) rotations are not [topologically mixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topologically_mixing).
- Irrational rotations are uniquely [ergodic](wikipedia://en/5456824), with the Lebesgue measure serving as the unique invariant probability measure.
- Suppose $[a, b] \subset [0, 1)$. Since $f_{\theta}$ is ergodic, $\text{lim} _ {N \to \infty} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \chi_{[a,b)}(f_\theta ^n (t))=b-a$.

:::

::: {#o7 .statement kind=statement/generalization cue=heading name="Generalizations"}

## Generalizations {#Generalizations}

- Circle rotations are examples of [group translations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation_%28group_theory%29).
- For a general orientation preserving homomorphism $f$ of $S^{1}$ to itself we call a homeomorphism $F:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$ a *lift* of $f$ if $\pi \circ F=f \circ \pi$ where $\pi (t)=t \bmod 1$.[^o12]
- The circle rotation can be thought of as a subdivision of a circle into two parts, which are then exchanged with each other. A subdivision into more than two parts, which are then permuted with one-another, is called an [interval exchange transformation](wikipedia://en/2606680).
- Rigid rotations of [compact groups](wikipedia://en/750326) effectively behave like circle rotations; the invariant measure is the [Haar measure](wikipedia://en/40645).

:::

::: {#o9 .application cue=heading name="Applications"}

## Applications {#Applications}

- Skew Products over Rotations of the Circle: In 1969[^o13] [William A. Veech](wikipedia://en/45548896) constructed examples of [minimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_%28mathematics%29) and not uniquely ergodic dynamical systems as follows: "Take two copies of the unit circle and mark off segment $J$ of length $2\pi\alpha$ in the counterclockwise direction on each one with endpoint at 0. Now take $\theta$ irrational and consider the following dynamical system. Start with a point $p$, say in the first circle. Rotate counterclockwise by $2\pi\theta$ until the first time the orbit lands in $J$; then switch to the corresponding point in the second circle, rotate by $2\pi\theta$ until the first time the point lands in $J$; switch back to the first circle and so forth. Veech showed that if $\theta$ is irrational, then there exists irrational $\alpha$ for which this system is minimal and the [Lebesgue measure](wikipedia://en/18198) is not uniquely ergodic."[^o14]

:::
